title: One shared audit platform with vendor AI at four mid-market firms
problem: Many mid-market firms run audits, reviews, compilations and benefit plan audits on disconnected tools with uneven methodology, and few build their own AI audit tooling.
approach: Firms adopt the AICPA-developed DAS suite on Caseware's platform, with the Caseware Verity AI assistant inside one shared engagement system.
Caseware says outputs are citation-backed and reviewable before entering the file; auditors accept, refine or override each suggestion (vendor-published).
Vendor-published adoption counts: Withum more than 1,000 active users and 6,000 engagements; EisnerAmper more than 1,100 professionals and 1,500 engagements.
Managers and partners review as before; no time, quality or cost results are published.
who: Withum, EisnerAmper, Citrin Cooperman, PKF O'Connor Davies

title: Standardise workpapers and the firm knowledge base before adding AI (Citrin Cooperman)
problem: Audit variability makes it hard for auditors to benefit from AI tools that need consistent execution, and occasional audits feel like starting over each time.
approach: Citrin Cooperman runs a dedicated project team to develop a standardised workpaper, layout and functionality, with technologists, experts, managers and quality teams.
The effort has run more than a year (self-reported); the article reports its length, not results.
A standardised knowledge base is meant to help AI surface the right information; the quality and standards teams help define the workpaper.

title: Test audit tools and AI agents on the firm's own engagements first
problem: Smaller firms depend on vendors' own accuracy statements; the only accuracy figures found for mid-market audit tools are vendor-run beta results.
approach: Thomson Reuters executives say leading firms compare systems side by side and run AI in parallel on live engagements (vendor-run interview).
Applied to an agent: score output against engagements with known answers, record misses by type, and re-test when the model changes.
Caseware reports 94% accuracy on golden dataset items from beta traces (vendor-published); no firm reports its own test result.
Partners decide whether the evidence is enough to scale; the methodology lead signs off results first.

title: Firm-built audit platforms starting with private-company audits (Grant Thornton, EisnerAmper)
problem: Firms with large private-company audit books want one data foundation and consistent workpapers across engagements instead of fragmented tools.
approach: Grant Thornton US announced gtap, a cloud platform standardising audit data and workpapers, rolling out to private-company audits first, then public-company audits.
EisnerAmper announced the EisnerAI Audit Design Agent, built with Microsoft, and also adopted DAS, so it both builds and buys.
Both firms describe intent only; neither gives accuracy, time or review-note figures (self-reported).
Auditors guide the process and keep oversight of agents.

title: Firm-built audit agents on vendor platforms, including overnight runs (FGMK, PKF)
problem: Firms want agents tailored to their own procedures, such as cash, journal entry and statement testing, without sending client data to open tools or building software.
approach: FGMK built DataSnipper Excel agents for cash, journal entry and statement testing, then tested Alwin, which runs overnight for next-morning review.
Preparer agents build workpapers and reviewer agents check statement consistency; FGMK's quality control team still runs its own independent review.
PKF O'Connor Davies joined Caseware's Agentic Pioneer Program to design its own agents; participation is announced, with no results published (vendor-published).
The reviewer sees the agent's steps beside the workbook and leaves cell-level notes.
who: FGMK, PKF O'Connor Davies, DataSnipper, Caseware

title: Named AI and technology leaders at private-company audit firms
problem: Tool adoption stalls without owners; firms name staff training, data access and budget as top blockers, and 75% of 54 surveyed firms have no formal transformation plan.
approach: Citrin Cooperman has an Assurance Innovation Leader; Withum a Team Leader, Digital Audit Solutions; EisnerAmper an Assurance Technology and Innovation Leader.
BPM advertised an Audit AI Technology Director to lead adoption, KPIs, change management and vendor budgets.
BW&O CPAs advertised an Audit Manager role to refine how auditors work with AI agents; it reviews workpapers and statements.
Job postings and titles show the roles exist (self-reported); no result is stated.
who: Citrin Cooperman, EisnerAmper, Withum, BPM, BW&O CPAs

title: Written AI use policy with approved tools and training for smaller firms
problem: Staff use general chat tools faster than firms write rules: more than one in three surveyed tax and audit professionals admit using unauthorised AI tools.
approach: The firm writes down approved tools, what client information may go in, the review standard for AI-assisted work, and a policy owner.
Tool access is tied to completed role-based training; the engagement partner confirms tools are firm-approved, used correctly and the team is competent.
Independent survey of 162 firms: 57% have a written, trained-on AI policy, up from 20% in 2024 (blog summary).
EisnerAmper and Citrin Cooperman used CPA.com for training and change management in their platform rollouts.

title: Write an AI transformation plan and baseline the metrics first
problem: 75% of 54 surveyed firms had no formal documentation of their audit transformation, and the metrics most track say little about AI's effect.
approach: Record a baseline before rollout (hours per task, review notes per file, nonconformity history) and track it afterwards.
The benchmark report suggests newer metrics, such as client readiness, and reinvesting a defined share of saved time (20% as an example).
Independent survey of 54 firms (not representative): only 28% track audit margin per engagement and 13% client readiness.
The practice leader reviews baseline and post-rollout figures together; a partner decides how much saved time is reinvested.

title: Start with general AI on low-risk drafting tasks (Beever and Struthers)
problem: Firms adopt general assistants without knowing whether time saved becomes output or whether staff trust the results, and risk being overwhelmed.
approach: Beever and Struthers introduced GenAI with skills sessions under a year-long university study; staff drafted emails, summarised documents and supported spreadsheet work.
A Caseware executive advised starting with easy tasks chosen with staff, not analytics, and reading licence terms (AICPA webcast).
Independent staff survey: 74% said GenAI helped them complete tasks faster; 22% reported a marked rise in overall output.
72% were concerned about incorrect output and 52% about client information handling; staff review all output.

title: Citation-backed research and document assistant for audit teams (Plante Moran)
problem: Audit teams lose time on technical research and on reading long unstructured documents such as board minutes, contracts and debt agreements, and staff are scarce.
approach: Thomson Reuters CoCounsel Audit gives citation-backed answers, accepts document uploads and lets firms integrate internal documents and templates.
Plante Moran piloted it with more than 140 participants; 91% said it was faster than traditional research, and access later widened (vendor-published).
Harris, Hardy & Johnstone says document review that took an hour now takes about five minutes (vendor-published).
The auditor reads the cited passages and decides what to rely on.

title: RSM's Luca audit ecosystem and Ask Luca guidance assistant
problem: Auditors serving middle-market clients need fast, firm-approved guidance in busy season and want to analyse more of the client's data.
approach: RSM added Ask Luca, generative AI over its assurance manuals and technical guides, to RSM Luca, used by 4,000+ assurance professionals.
The ecosystem also uses AI for risk-focused data analysis, journal-entry visualisations, matching source documents to support data, and statement review and validation.
RSM says Ask Luca reduces research time (self-reported); no timing or accuracy figure is given.
Auditors apply professional judgment and critical thinking to the outputs.

title: Client request intake: agents validate client submissions and extract data into workpapers
problem: Client information arrives late, incomplete or poorly formatted, and staff retype PDFs into Excel; 60% of 54 firms ranked poor-quality client data among top blockers.
approach: Caseware Client Requests feeds client information into the Excel workpaper; a validation agent checks it and the auditor accepts or rejects each.
Caseware's Document Intelligence Agent, in beta in June 2026, extracts source-document information into workpapers; Client Requests is in limited early access.
Suralink's Extract Links structures data from client documents and Link Answers answers lease and debt agreement questions, each tied to its source.
Announcements and beta descriptions only (vendor-published); no customer, hours or accuracy figure.

title: Proof of cash for small-business clients without ERP data feeds
problem: Clients keep books in QuickBooks, Xero and similar systems, hand over inconsistent exports and PDF bank statements, and often refuse direct API access.
approach: Audit Sight sits over the engagement platform, takes data by read-only connection or Excel and CSV templates, and converts PDF bank statements.
It rebuilds a complete general ledger and produces a proof-of-cash workpaper reconciling every bank and book transaction.
A Holbrook & Manter partner says automated cash testing changed how the firm does substantive testing (vendor-published); no hours or error figures.
The auditor investigates unreconciled items and concludes; the output is a workpaper input, not the conclusion.
who: Holbrook & Manter, Audit Sight, Thomson Reuters

title: Risk-focused sample selection recorded as a workpaper (Sam Brown CPA)
problem: A small firm relied on Excel templates and manual steps for sampling, testing and documentation, over-audited, and found it hard to justify leaner samples to peer reviewers.
approach: Thomson Reuters Audit Intelligence Analyze runs transaction analytics inside the workflow to focus procedures on higher-risk areas.
Selections are recorded as workpapers, so the firm can show peer reviewers why a sample is the size it is.
The owner estimates at least five to six hours saved per audit (vendor-published); an estimate, not a tracked metric.
The firm decides which selections to test; peer review of the file follows.

title: Excel assistant drafting workpapers and test steps from the audit file (Caseware)
problem: Auditors move information by hand between the audit file, client submissions and Excel workpapers; Caseware's aim is less time searching for and transferring information.
approach: Caseware says Verity for Excel reads the connected engagement from inside Excel and runs multi-step workflows for workpaper generation and test automation.
It covers tests of controls, substantive analytics and tests of details; Caseware described it as generally available on 9 September 2026.
Caseware reports, from its own testing to date, an average of 9 hours saved per engagement and 75% per task (vendor-published).
The practitioner approves each suggested change before it is applied.

title: AI gap flagging and cross-file checks aimed at recurring small-firm peer-review findings
problem: Small firms feel quality-management and peer-review compliance effort now rivals audit work, and peer reviews show weak risk assessment documentation linked to procedures.
approach: The AICPA column advises standardising templates and checklists and says audit AI can help identify gaps and flag inconsistencies earlier (column claim).
Thomson Reuters argues traceable links from planning to risk to procedure to conclusion reduce deficiencies reviewers look for (vendor claim).
Caseware describes cross-file risk checks; its demo surfaced a trial-balance variance with no associated risk. No peer-review result is reported.
Manager and partner remain the reviewers, with engagement quality review where required.

title: Compilation and review engagements on the same AI-enabled platform as audits
problem: Reviews and compilations are high-volume at small firms; in 2025 state peer-review reports, 43 of 295 reviews (15%) were nonconforming, and no AI-specific practice material was found.
approach: Citrin Cooperman, Withum and EisnerAmper adopted the DAS suite including its compilation and review module, which makes no AI claim.
Caseware's Disclosure Checklist Agent is described only in the audit workflow; AI inside compilation and review work is not described.
Adoption counts cover the whole suite (EisnerAmper: more than 1,100 professionals, over 1,500 engagements; vendor-published), not an AI effect on compilations.
The accountant reviews and signs the compilation or review report.

title: Decide and explain where AI savings go: margin, fees or value
problem: Efficiency gains in audits can be competed away through fees, CFOs are asking where savings go, and finance leaders are split on whether auditor AI improved quality.
approach: A small firm says freed capacity served more clients without fee rises; another says it can maintain or raise rates (vendor-published).
Of 54 benchmark firms, 74% anticipate raising fees, 13% track value-billing agreements and 66% tell clients about their technology (independent).
FERF advises finance leaders to ask their auditor how AI affects scope, fees or insight; partners approve pricing for AI-shortened work.
The engagement partner owns the conversation with the CFO or audit committee.
who: FERF, CPA.com and AICPA, Thomson Reuters

title: Idea: tell your liability insurer how AI is used and check exclusions
problem: Idea, not a deployment: insurers say errors from unvetted AI output can be covered like any error unless a policy excludes AI, and exclusions may come if claims rise.
approach: Idea: the firm asks its broker about any AI exclusion or sublimit, and tells the insurer how AI is used.
Idea: keep the policy, review and consent records that show AI output was verified.
A CNA risk director says the lack of a CPA-specific AI standard is unlikely to help defend an inadequate-review claim.
The managing partner reviews coverage at each renewal.

title: Idea: continuous, AI-run audits sold by start-ups, challenging hours-based fees
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: audit fees and delivery models are built on labour-intensive procedures.
approach: Idea: new entrants run continuous, AI-driven audits that undercut the hours-based model.
A machine-written summary of a September 2026 podcast says start-ups such as Oath Verified are pioneering continuous AI-powered audits, with no data.
The summary does not say whether any private-company audit has been signed under this model.
The source states no human checkpoint; the opinion still rests with a licensed auditor under existing standards.
